title: Synthetic Acute Systemic Infection Assessment Reference
passages: In a synthetic acute-care case, a converging pattern of fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis, elevated lactate, and hypotension should trigger urgent clinician review for systemic infection and associated organ dysfunction rather than being interpreted from any single measurement.
A sepsis-like pattern requires assessment for a plausible infection source, organ dysfunction, hemodynamic deterioration, and competing non-infectious causes of shock or systemic inflammation.

Worsening hypotension, rising lactate, hypoxemia, or other signs of physiologic deterioration are high-risk findings that should be escalated to direct human clinical assessment; this prototype must not initiate treatment or replace emergency evaluation.

title: Synthetic Respiratory Assessment Reference
passages: For a synthetic adult case with cough, fever, and dyspnea, review respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, lung examination findings, and the overall severity pattern before narrowing the differential.

A focal opacity or consolidation described on chest imaging can support a lower respiratory infectious pattern when it is concordant with symptoms, but imaging findings should be interpreted together with history, examination, and laboratory context.
Respiratory infection patterns can overlap with viral illness and non-infectious cardiopulmonary conditions; contradictory findings and alternative explanations should remain visible during review.

title: Synthetic Viral Respiratory Illness Reference
passages: Fever and cough may occur in viral respiratory illness. Exposure history, upper-respiratory symptoms, local epidemiology, and relevant testing can help distinguish viral from other respiratory patterns in a synthetic case.
A viral hypothesis should be reconsidered when strong focal findings or another coherent explanation better account for the available evidence.

title: Synthetic Dyspnea Differential Reference
passages: Shortness of breath has infectious and non-infectious causes. Synthetic case review can include cardiac history, volume-status findings, thromboembolic risk factors, ECG findings, and other discriminating information when relevant.
A challenge step should explicitly check whether fever or inflammatory findings sufficiently explain dyspnea or whether a competing cardiopulmonary process remains plausible.

title: Synthetic Chest Pain Assessment Reference
passages: For a synthetic chest-pain presentation, potentially important cardiac causes should remain in consideration until discriminating history, ECG findings, biomarkers, and risk context are reviewed.
Musculoskeletal chest pain becomes more plausible when pain is reproducible with palpation or movement, but those findings should be explicitly documented rather than assumed.

title: Synthetic Diagnostic Decision-Support Safety Reference
passages: When available information is incomplete, the decision-support system should surface uncertainty and missing information instead of inventing patient facts or presenting a definitive diagnosis.
All diagnostic hypotheses and next-step suggestions produced by this prototype require explicit clinician review before any real-world action.

title: Synthetic Acute Heart Failure Assessment Reference
passages: In a synthetic dyspnea case, a pattern of known heart failure, progressive orthopnea, peripheral edema, elevated natriuretic peptide, cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines, interstitial edema, or bilateral pleural effusions supports review for acute heart-failure decompensation while precipitating causes remain open.

Heart-failure decompensation should be challenged for alternative or precipitating processes such as ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, pulmonary embolic disease, medication non-adherence, or a hypertensive surge when the record contains discriminating clues.
Hypoxemia, hypotension, marked tachypnea, worsening renal function, or other physiologic deterioration in a heart-failure presentation should prompt urgent human clinical assessment.

title: Synthetic Acute Coronary Syndrome Assessment Reference
passages: For a synthetic chest-pain case, pressure-like discomfort, radiation, diaphoresis, ischemic ECG changes, elevated cardiac biomarkers, and vascular risk factors support consideration of acute coronary syndrome while alternative chest-pain causes remain visible.

Serial ECG and cardiac-biomarker trends can help distinguish an evolving ischemic process from non-ischemic chest pain in a synthetic diagnostic workflow; the prototype should not issue treatment orders.
Atypical symptoms do not by themselves exclude ischemia, particularly when objective ECG or biomarker findings support myocardial injury.

title: Synthetic Pulmonary Embolism Assessment Reference
passages: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, unilateral leg swelling, and recent immobility or prolonged travel can support consideration of pulmonary embolic disease in a synthetic case.

A pulmonary embolism hypothesis should be compared with pneumonia, acute heart failure, pneumothorax, and other cardiopulmonary explanations using the available imaging, infection findings, volume-status clues, and thromboembolic risk context.
Hypoxemia or hemodynamic deterioration in a suspected thromboembolic presentation is a high-risk finding requiring direct clinician assessment.

title: Synthetic Obstructive Airway Exacerbation Reference
passages: In a synthetic COPD case, increased dyspnea, sputum volume or purulence, wheeze, hyperinflation, hypoxemia, or hypercapnia can support an acute exacerbation while focal consolidation or another competing cause should be considered separately.

In a synthetic asthma case, episodic wheeze, chest tightness, exposure-related onset, reduced peak expiratory flow, increased work of breathing, and tachypnea support an acute asthma exacerbation pattern.
Obstructive-airway presentations should retain alternative explanations such as pneumonia, heart failure, pulmonary embolic disease, or pneumothorax when the record contains discordant features.

title: Synthetic Hyperglycemic Crisis Assessment Reference
passages: A synthetic case with diabetes, marked hyperglycemia, positive ketones, low bicarbonate, acidemia, and an elevated anion gap supports consideration of diabetic ketoacidosis.

Vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dehydration, and deep rapid respirations can accompany a hyperglycemic ketoacidotic pattern and should not automatically be assigned to a primary gastrointestinal or pulmonary disorder.
Missing medication, infection, ischemia, or other precipitating information should be surfaced as an unresolved question rather than inferred.

title: Synthetic Renal and Electrolyte Assessment Reference
passages: A synthetic case with recent fluid loss, hypotension or dehydration findings, reduced urine output, and a creatinine rise from baseline supports consideration of volume-depletion-associated prerenal acute kidney injury while other renal causes remain open.
Markedly elevated potassium together with compatible ECG abnormalities such as peaked T waves or QRS widening supports consideration of clinically important hyperkalemia in a synthetic record.
Renal and electrolyte findings should be interpreted with medication history, baseline kidney function, volume status, and other possible causes rather than from an isolated laboratory value.

title: Synthetic Acute Neurologic Assessment Reference
passages: Sudden focal neurologic deficits such as unilateral weakness, facial droop, aphasia, or visual change support urgent review for an acute cerebrovascular event in a synthetic case.
A non-contrast head CT without hemorrhage does not by itself exclude early ischemia; timing, focal examination findings, glucose, and competing mimics remain important to diagnostic reasoning.
Hypoglycemia can cause confusion or neurologic symptoms and should remain visible as a reversible stroke mimic when low glucose is explicitly documented.

title: Synthetic Central Nervous System Infection Reference
passages: A synthetic presentation combining fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, or altered mental status supports consideration of meningitis or another central nervous system infection.

The reasoning process should distinguish meningitis from migraine, subarachnoid hemorrhage, encephalitis, and other causes using the documented neurologic examination, systemic findings, and relevant testing.
Hypotension, marked physiologic deterioration, or other systemic red flags in a suspected CNS infection require urgent direct clinician assessment.

title: Synthetic Gastrointestinal Bleeding Assessment Reference
passages: Coffee-ground emesis, hematemesis, melena, anemia, or compatible risk factors support consideration of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in a synthetic case.
Dizziness, syncope, tachycardia, hypotension, falling hemoglobin, or other evidence of physiologic compromise should be surfaced as severity findings rather than treated as isolated symptoms.
The differential should keep alternative bleeding sources and non-bleeding explanations visible when the presentation is incomplete.

title: Synthetic Acute Abdominal Assessment Reference
passages: Migration of abdominal pain toward the right lower quadrant with anorexia, leukocytosis, and imaging showing an enlarged inflamed appendix supports consideration of acute appendicitis in a synthetic case.

Persistent right upper-quadrant pain with fever, leukocytosis, gallstones, gallbladder-wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, or a sonographic Murphy sign supports consideration of acute cholecystitis rather than uncomplicated biliary colic.

Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with a markedly elevated lipase and compatible pancreatic imaging supports consideration of acute pancreatitis while cardiac and other abdominal alternatives remain visible.

title: Synthetic Urinary Infection Assessment Reference
passages: Fever, flank pain, urinary symptoms, costovertebral-angle tenderness, pyuria, nitrites, leukocyte esterase, or leukocytosis can support consideration of acute pyelonephritis in a synthetic case.
Vomiting or abdominal discomfort can accompany an upper urinary infection and should be interpreted with urinary findings rather than assumed to represent a primary gastrointestinal disorder.
Hypotension, elevated lactate, or other systemic deterioration in a urinary-infection presentation should trigger urgent clinician review.

title: Synthetic Endocrine and Glucose Assessment Reference
passages: Heat intolerance, tremor, weight loss, palpitations, tachycardia, suppressed TSH, and elevated free thyroid hormone levels can support consideration of thyrotoxicosis in a synthetic case.

Documented low blood glucose in a patient with confusion, diaphoresis, weakness, or neurologic symptoms supports consideration of symptomatic hypoglycemia and should be compared with competing neurologic explanations.
Endocrine findings should remain grounded in documented laboratory and clinical data; severity labels or precipitating factors should not be invented.

title: Synthetic Acute Aortic Syndrome Reference
passages: Abrupt severe chest or back pain described as tearing, a pulse deficit or inter-arm blood-pressure difference, and mediastinal widening can support consideration of acute aortic syndrome in a synthetic case.
Acute aortic syndrome can overlap with acute coronary syndrome and other chest-pain causes; discriminating vascular examination and imaging findings should remain explicit in the reasoning trace.
The decision-support system should surface the potentially high-risk alternative without making an autonomous final diagnosis.

title: Synthetic Non-Ischemic Cardiac Chest Pain Reference
passages: Sharp pleuritic chest pain that worsens when supine and improves when leaning forward, together with diffuse ST-segment elevation or PR depression, can support consideration of acute pericarditis in a synthetic case.
Diffuse rather than territorial ECG changes, positional symptoms, biomarker context, and recent viral illness can help distinguish pericarditis from acute myocardial infarction.
The differential should keep ischemic and other dangerous chest-pain causes visible until the available evidence is reconciled.
